item.title: Solved: How to Fix ValueError Unknown Projection '3d' in Matplotlib
item.description:
Question:

Encountering the error ValueError: Unknown projection ‘3d’ can be frustrating, especially when attempting to run example scripts from Matplotlib after a fresh installation. Below is an example script where users frequently get stuck.

from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import axes3d
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.gca(projection='3d')
X, Y, Z = axes3d.get_test_data(0.05)
cset = ax.contour(X, Y, Z, 16, extend3d=True)
ax.clabel(cset, fontsize=9, inline=1)

plt.show()

The above code can lead to the following traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  raise ValueError("Unknown projection '%s'" % projection)
ValueError: Unknown projection '3d'

Solutions:

Solution 1: Update or Verify Matplotlib Version

The primary reason for the ValueError: Unknown projection ‘3d’ is typically related to the version of Matplotlib you are using. Older versions of Matplotlib handle 3D plotting differently.

item.title: Solved: Why Do Many Examples Use fig, ax = plt.subplots()?
item.description:
I’m diving into the functionality of Matplotlib as I learn through various examples, and I’ve noticed a recurring pattern: many examples make use of the line:

fig, ax = plt.subplots()

This pattern seems to appear frequently even in cases where only a single plot is being generated. Here’s a snapshot of the way this function is typically employed:

Example: Creating a Simple Plot

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [10, 20, 25, 30]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_title('Simple Plot')
plt.show()

Notably, the official Matplotlib demo consistently uses the fig, ax = plt.subplots() format for single chart generation. You might wonder: Is there an inherent advantage to this approach? Let’s explore the uses and benefits of plt.subplots(), along with various solutions to maximize its potential.

item.title: Top 10 Methods to Solve Tight Layout Issues with Matplotlib Suptitles
item.description:
If you’ve ever grappled with the issue of your matplotlib figure’s suptitle overlapping with subplot titles, you’re not alone. Many users face the challenge of using the tight_layout() function, only to find that it often exacerbates the problem rather than resolving it. Below, we delve into some practical and innovative methods to overcome this issue and ensure that your visualizations are both aesthetically pleasing and informative.

Why Does Tight Layout Fail with Suptitle?

The issue stems from the fact that tight_layout() does not account for the space occupied by fig.suptitle(). As a result, when you add a subtitle to your figure, it can end up obscured by the titles of the subplots. This problem has been documented in GitHub issues and further discussions on related topics.
